title: Women Ancestors, Known and Unknown
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart reads from the Therigatha, the poems of the elder nuns, and tells the stories of two women, Ambapali and Kisa Gotami. Kanho describes Ambapali, the celebrated courtesan of Vesali, who wins the Buddha's meal over the Licchavi nobles because she was there first, then reads her poem cataloguing the losses of age, each verse closing on the refrain that the truth speaker's words do not change. Kisa Gotami carries her dead child from house to house in search of a mustard seed from a home untouched by death, and finds none. In the discussion that follows, one participant hears Ambapali's refrain as a victory song.

sentences.text: *An answered path penetrating in perfect dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Is this recording?
Better not turn it off then, huh?
Good evening, friends.
Women ancestors known and unknown.
That's really falling right into what I would love to talk about tonight.
We're continuing our conversation about our feminine Buddhist ancestors.
Because of that, I will again stray from the traditional transmission of the lamp or transmission of light, which describes our male ancestors in great detail.
I turned to the poems of the elder nuns, the Terigata.
The Terigata are a poem collection from men and women who lived in the time of the Buddha.
The nuns' collection is called Terigata, and the collection of the monks is called Teragata.
They lived over 2,500 years ago, yet their experiences and their teaching are as relevant today as they were then.
In our own lives, we encounter challenges, attachments, and the relentless cycle of desire and suffering.
We may not have exactly the same circumstances as the nuns, but the path of awakening still speaks to our hearts.
We will tonight hear about two women, Amma Pali and Kisa Gotami.
There is universality in their teaching.
Whether we are lay people or monastics, no matter what the gender, we all face the same existential questions.
Who am I?
Why do I suffer?
Why does this hurt so much?
How can I be free?
The answers that the nuns offer are not abstract or theoretical.
They are real, lived experience.
They invite us to practice with sincerity, to reflect on our attachments, and to cultivate wisdom through mindfulness and insight.
In our modern, busy lives, we can sometimes feel overwhelmed by life, by our wants, our desires, by things going wrong.
But just as these nuns faced similar struggles and overcame them through sustained effort and practice, we too can follow their example.
Whether it is through meditation or studying the Dharma or engaging in acts of compassion, the way forward is clear.
The stories of these elder nuns are an invitation to practice without hesitation.
They did not wait for the perfect conditions to begin their practice.
They were ordinary women in most cases, facing the challenges and difficulties of life.
Yet they did not let those challenges define them.
They didn't let their past hold them back.
They embraced the teachings of the Buddha, and through them they transcended the suffering that plagued them and all sentient beings.

The Terigata encourages us to reflect on our own attachments, to look deeply into the impermanence of things, and to see that true liberation is not found in external circumstances, but in the inner transformation of wisdom and letting go.
I would like to start with the story of Amma Pali.
When Manudev, the king of Vesali, saw Amma Pali perform a dance, he admired her so much that he declared Amma Pali as a bride of Vesali and a court dancer.
Due to her extraordinary beauty, Amma Pali became a Nagarvado, a courtesan, a role that was both respected and controversial in ancient Indian society.
As the most sought after courtesan in Vesali, she was admired by kings, nobles, and wealthy merchants.
She did have the right to choose her lovers as the bride of Vesali, however she was not allowed to marry and to commit to one person and one family.
Her talent and beauty attracted so many that the glory of Vesali during this period is often attributed to Amma Pali's fame.
She amassed great wealth and influence, living a life of luxury.
The price to meet with Amma Pali was so high that her treasury exceeded that of many kings.
It is quite remarkable that this beautiful woman became the Buddha's follower.
Despite her external success, Amma Pali must have felt a sense of emptiness and dissatisfaction.
The fleeting nature of pleasure and the superficiality of her life must have weighed on her.
The following is an excerpt from the Mahaparanibbana Sutta, The Last Days of the Buddha.
The events I'm going to read about happen towards the end of the Buddha's life, so I'm setting the scene.
Amma Pali heard that the Buddha was in Vesali and he was staying at her grove.
That's a place the Buddha often used when he was in Vesali.
He and the monks lived there basically.
So she had the best carriages made ready and drove from Vesali to her park.
*She drove as far as the ground would allow, then alighted and went on foot to where the Lord was.
She saluted the Lord and sat down to one side.
And as she sat, the Lord instructed, inspired, fired, and delighted her with a talk on Dhamma.
And being thus delighted, Amma Pali said, "Lord, may the Lord consent to take a meal from me tomorrow with his order of monks."
The Lord consented by silence, and Amma Pali, understanding his acceptance, rose from her seat, saluted the Lord, and, passing him by to the right, departed.*
I'm going to abbreviate the next passage, though it's a lot of fun.
As she is taking off back to her house, the noblemen of the Djavi tribe came the other direction.
She must have had this kind of comeuppance aura.
They're saying, "Why are you driving up against us like this?"
And she says, "Because, young sirs, the Blessed Lord has been invited by me for a meal with his order of monks."
The noblemen shout at her, "Amma Pali, give up this meal for a hundred thousand pieces of gold."
And she replies, "Young sirs, if you were to give me all this Vesali, with its revenues, I would not give up such an important meal."
And the Djavi snapped their fingers.
That probably means they were kind of upset.
And they said, "We have been beaten by a mango woman."
That was probably somewhat derogatory.
"We've been cheated by the mango woman."
And they said, I'm out for Amma Pali's grove to meet with the Buddha too.
Then they pretend that they haven't met Amma Pali, and they say, "Lord, may the Lord consent to take a meal from us tomorrow with his order of monks."
And the Buddha replies, "But the Djavis, I have already accepted a meal for tomorrow from the courtesan Amma Pali."
And the Djavis snapped their fingers saying, "We've been beaten by the mango woman."
"We've been cheated by the mango woman."
And they said, "Why are you taking her offer?
She's a courtesan.
We're the Lords."
And the Buddha says, "Because she was there first."
This is one of the stories that give me great delight.
At the end of the meal, by the way, she offered the Buddha and his order that entire park and grove as a gift.
It was Amma Pali's grove.
And soon after this, she renounced her position as a courtesan and court dancer and accepted the Buddhist way and remained an active supporter of the Buddhist Sangha.
She also dedicated her life to service of the poor.
So this is her contribution in the Terikata.
*Black was my hair, the color of bees, and curled at the tips.
With age it looked like coarse hemp.
The truth of the truth speaker's words does not change.
Fragrant like a perfume basket filled with flowers.
With age it smelled musty like animal fur.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.*

The tips elaborate with comb and pin.
The truth of the truth speaker's words does not change.
Adorned with gold and delicate pins, it was splendid, ornamented with braids.
Now with age the head has gone bald.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Curved as if well-drawn by an artist, my brows were once splendid.
With age they droop down in folds.*
*The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Radiant, brilliant like jewels, my eyes.
With age they are no longer splendid.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Like a delicate peak, my nose was splendid in the prime of my youth.
With age it's like a long pepper.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Like bracelets well-fashioned, well-finished, my ears were once splendid.*
*With age they droop down in folds.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Like plantain buds in their color, my teeth were once splendid.
With age they are broken and yellowed.
The truth of the truth speaker's words does not change.
Like that of a cuckoo in the dense jungle, flitting through deep forest thickets.
Sweet was the tone of my voice.
With age it cracks here and there.*
*The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Smooth like a conch shell, well-polished, my neck was once splendid.
With age it's broken down, bent.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Like rounded door bars, both of them, my arms were once splendid.
With age they're like dried up potali trees.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Adorned with gold and delicate rings, my hands were once splendid.*
*With age they are like onions and tubers.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Swelling round, firm and high, both my breasts were once splendid.
In the drought of old age they dangle like empty old water bags.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Like a sheet of gold, well-burnished, my body was splendid.
Now it's covered with very fine wrinkles.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.*
*Smooth in their lines, like an elephant's trunk, both my thighs were once splendid.
With age they're like knotted bamboo.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
Adorned with gold and delicate anklets, my calves were once splendid.
With age they're like sesame sticks.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.
As if they were stuffed with soft cotton, both my feet were once splendid.
With age they're shriveled and cracked.*
*The truth of the truth speaker's words does not change.
Such was this physical heap.
Now a house with its plaster all fallen off.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.*
I'll just repeat that last stanza.
*Such was this physical heap.
Now a house with its plaster all fallen off.
The truth of the truth speaker's words doesn't change.*
The next story is the story of Kisa Gotami.
Kisa Gotami's story is one of deep sorrow and profound awakening.
Kisa Gotami was a young woman from a wealthy family who was married to a man from Swavasti.
She was very happy when they had a child.
And she really loved that boy.
However the baby fell ill and died.
Overcome with grief and unable to accept the death of her child, Kisa Gotami refused to let go of the body.
In her despair she carried the body, the dead body of her child, with her wherever she went.
She asked help from everyone around her.
But no one could help and no one could console her.
Her sorrow was so great that she lost her mind.
Finally someone advised her to seek out the Buddha, who was known for his wisdom and ability to alleviate suffering.
In her state of deep sorrow, Kisa Gotami went to the Buddha holding her dead child.
She asked him for a remedy.
The Buddha, seeing her pain, told her, yes, I can help.
But only if she could bring him a mustard seed from a household that had not experienced death.
A mustard seed is like this tiny little insignificant thing.
Everybody had it in their house.
Desperate, Kisa Gotami went from house to house asking for a mustard seed.
But everywhere she went, she encountered people who had lost someone close to them.
Whether it was a child, a spouse, a sibling, a friend, everyone had experienced death.
Kisa Gotami slowly realized that death was a universal part of life, touching everyone regardless of wealth, status, or position in society.
With this understanding, Kisa Gotami returned to the Buddha, where she acknowledged the impermanence of life and the inevitability of death.
She let go of her child's body and, deeply moved by the Buddha's teaching, became one of his followers.
Kisa Gotami renounced the world and entered the monastic life as a nun.
Through her profound grief and the Buddha's teaching, Kisa Gotami's heart opened.
She meditated deeply and gained wisdom and enlightenment.
Kisa Gotami's story is often seen as a teaching on the impermanence of life and the importance of letting go.
Her transformation from deep sorrow to spiritual wisdom is a powerful reminder that suffering can be a catalyst for growth and enlightenment.
Kisa Gotami's journey highlights the Buddhist path of acceptance, understanding, and ultimate liberation from the cycle of suffering.
Her story, especially the universality of death, resonates deeply with many followers of Buddhism to this day, encouraging us to understand that death is universal and loss is a part of life.
*This is the poem she left us.
Having admirable friends has been praised by the sage with reference to the world.
Associating with an admirable friend, even a fool, becomes wise.
People of integrity should be associated with.
In that way, discernment grows.
Associating with people of integrity, one would be released from all suffering and stress, with no stress, the origination of stress, cessation and the eightfold path, the Four Noble Truth.

Being a co-wife is painful.*

Going along, about to give birth, I saw my husband, dead.
Giving birth in the road, I hadn't reached my own home.
Two children deceased, my husband dead in the road, miserable me.
My mother, father and brother were burning on a single pyre.
Your family, all gone, miserable.*
*You've suffered great pain without measure.
Your tears have flowed for many thousands of lives.
Then I saw, in the midst of the charnel ground, the muscles of sons being chewed.
This family killed, despised by all, my husband dead.
I reached the deathless.
I've developed this path, Noble Eightfold, going to the deathless.
Having realized unbinding, I've gazed in the mirror of dharma.
I've cut out the arrow, put down the burden, done the task.*
*I, Kisa Gotami Terry, my heart well released, have said this.*

Kisa Gotami was a young woman from a healthy family who was married to a man from Swavasti. She was very happy when they had a child. And she really loved that boy. However the baby fell ill and died. Overcome with grief and unable to accept the death of her child, Kisa Gotami refused to let go of the body.

In her despair she carried the body, the dead body of her child with her wherever she went. And she asked help from everyone around her. But no one could help and no one could console her. Her sorrow was so great that she lost her mind. Finally someone advised her to seek out the Buddha who was known for his wisdom and ability to alleviate suffering. In her state of deep sorrow, Kisa Gotami went to the Buddha holding her dead child. She asked him for a remedy. The Buddha seeing her pain told her, yes, I can help.

But only if she could bring him a mustard seed from a household that had not experienced death. A mustard seed is like this tiny little insignificant thing. Everybody had it in their house. Desperate, Kisa Gotami went from house to house asking for a mustard seed. But everywhere she went, she encountered people who had lost someone close to them. Whether it was a child, a spouse, a sibling, a friend, everyone had experienced death. Kisa Gotami slowly realized that death was a universal part of life, touching everyone regardless of wealth, status, or position in society. With this understanding, Kisa Gotami returned to the Buddha where she acknowledged the impermanence of life and the inevitability of death.

She let go of her child's body and, deeply moved by the Buddha's teaching, became one of his followers. Kisa Gotami renounced the world and entered the monastic life as a nun. Through her profound grief and the Buddha's teaching, Kisa Gotami's heart opened. She meditated deeply and gained wisdom and enlightenment. Kisa Gotami's story is often seen as a teaching on the impermanence of life and the importance of letting go. Her transformation from deep sorrow to spiritual wisdom is a powerful reminder that suffering can be a catalyst for growth and enlightenment. Kisa Gotami's journey highlights the Buddhist path of acceptance, understanding, and ultimate liberation from the cycle of suffering. Her story, especially the universality of death, resonates deeply with many followers of Buddhism to this day, encouraging us to understand that death is universal and loss is a part of life.
